title: Part Two, Chapter 6: The Cornfield and the Rat

verses.t: And when they began their works and to show themselves before their grandmother and their mother, the first thing they set about was to make a cornfield. "We shall plant a cornfield," they said to their grandmother and their mother. "Do not grieve; here we are, your grandsons; we are the replacements of our brothers." This is what Hun-ahpu and Xbalanque said. And then, taking their axes and hoes, they went off with their blowguns on their shoulders; and as they left their house they told their grandmother to bring them their food at midday. "Very well, my grandsons," said the old woman. And when they came to the field where they were to plant, they drove the hoe into the ground, and the hoe by itself tilled a great deal; and driving the axe into a tree, all the trees went falling flat, and all the vines too. And there was a great quantity of trees felled and cut with only one axe and only one hoe; a great deal had already been tilled. All that they had done with a single stroke of the hoe in all the hills, small and great, could not be counted; everything came down. And then they gave orders to an animal called Xmucur (that is, the wild dove), and set it on top of a stump, and Hun-ahpu and Xbalanque said to it, "Watch for when our grandmother comes, for she is to come and bring us food, and sing at once when you see her coming, and at once we shall take up our hoe and axe." "Very well," said the dove. And then they only amused themselves shooting with the blowgun, and paid no attention to the cornfield. And as soon as the dove sang, they came in great haste: one took the hoe and the other the axe, and tying up their heads, they smeared their hands with earth for show: the one as if dirtying his face like a man who plants corn, and the other, for show, scattering wood chips on his head like a woodcutter. And then their grandmother saw them, and they ate; they were not really making the cornfield, and so the food was brought to them for nothing. And then they went home. "Truly we are tired, grandmother," they said to her; and coming to their house they made a show of their labour, stretching their hands and feet before their grandmother and rubbing them. And then they went on the second day, and when they came to the field they found all the trees and vines standing up again; they had joined and come together again. "Who can it be," they said, "that has tricked us? No doubt the ones who did this are all the animals, great and small: the jaguar, the deer, the rabbit, the wildcat, the coyote, the peccary, the coati, and the birds, great and small; these are the ones who did this." And then they set to making the cornfield again, and the earth and the cut trees did as before. And then they took counsel over the felled trees and the cleared ground: "We shall keep watch over our cornfield; perhaps we shall catch whoever comes to do this." This is what they said in their counsel, and they came home. "What do you think, grandmother, of what we have seen, the trick they have played on us? What we tilled has turned back into forest and grassland; we found it like that when we went just now." This is what they said to their grandmother and their mother. "We shall go back again and keep watch, for this that they have done to us is not good." So they said; and then they armed themselves and went back to their clearing. And then they hid themselves, and were hidden there, when all the animals gathered; all the animals, small and great, gathered in one place, and then at the stroke of midnight they came. And speaking all together as they came, they said, "Yachisché, Yachiscaam" (that is: "Rise up, trees; rise up, vines"). This is what they said as they came, and they moved about beneath the trees and vines. Coming nearer, they showed themselves before the boys. And the first were a puma and a jaguar, and the boys tried to catch them, but they would not let themselves be caught. And then a deer and a rabbit came close, and the boys closed in together and caught them, but only their tails came off; so they took the tail of the deer and the tail of the rabbit, and that is why their tails are so short. And neither the wildcat nor the coyote, nor the peccary nor the coati, would let themselves be caught; all the animals passed in front of Hun-ahpu and Xbalanque, and their hearts were bursting with anger because they had not caught any. And at the very last one came leaping along, and cutting it off, they caught the rat in a net. And as soon as they caught it, they squeezed its head and tried to choke it, and they burned its tail in the fire; and so the rat got its hairless tail, and its bulging eyes too, when the two boys Hun-ahpu and Xbalanque tried to choke it. And the rat said, "Do not kill me; making cornfields is not your calling." "Then what is it you are telling us?" the two boys said to the rat. "Let me go a little, for I have something in my belly to tell, and I shall tell it afterwards. Give me something to eat," said the rat. And it was said to it, "We shall give you your food afterwards; tell it now." "Very well," said the rat. "You must know that the things of your fathers, Hun-hun-ahpu and Vucub-hun-ahpu, as those were called who died in the underworld, are there; the things they played with are hanging up in the loft: their yoke, the bat and the rubber ball. And your grandmother will not show them to you, because it was through these that your fathers died." And the boys said, "Do you really know this?" And they rejoiced greatly when they heard the news of the rubber ball. And when the rat had spoken, they assigned the rat its food: "This shall be your food: maize, chile seeds, beans, pataxte, cacao; this is yours. And if anything is stored away or forgotten, that is yours too; eat it." This was said to the rat by Hun-ahpu and Xbalanque. "Very well, boys. But will your grandmother not see me? What do you say to that?" said the rat. "Do not worry, for we are here, and we shall see to what must be done. Ah, we shall speak to our grandmother as soon as we have put you in the corner of the house, when we arrive. Get at once to where it is hanging, and there we shall look at the ground chile for our food, and we shall see," they said to the rat. And then they made their plans for the night; and Hun-ahpu and Xbalanque took counsel, and they arrived at midday.

And they were carrying the rat hidden; and when they arrived, one went straight into the house and the other to the corner, and at once he lifted the rat up high and put it there. And then they asked their grandmother for their food. "Grind our food, for we want chile sauce, grandmother." This is what they said; and then their chile was ground and a bowl of broth was set before them. But this was to deceive the old woman and their mother: they drained the water that was in the jar, and said, "We are dying of thirst. Go, bring water," they said to their grandmother. "Good," she said, and then she went for the water, and they stayed eating. But in truth they were not hungry; it was only a trick they were playing. And then they saw the rat in the chile sauce: the rat was free, up at the chile that hung in the loft, and they saw it reflected in the chile or chile sauce. And then they sent a little creature called Xan, which is like a mosquito, and it went to the water or the stream and pierced the old woman's water jar, and the water ran out of the jar; she tried, but the hole in the jar could not be stopped. "What can our grandmother be doing? We are drying up with thirst," they said to their mother. "Go, lady, and see." And they sent her off. And then the rat gnawed through where the rubber ball hung, and the bat and the yoke, and they fell; and the boys snatched them up and went and hid them on the road, which is the road to the ball court, the place where they played ball. And then they went to where their grandmother was; and their grandmother and their mother were each busy stopping the hole in the jar. And they arrived, each with his blowgun, at the water. "What have you been doing? We got tired of waiting, so we came." "Look at my jar," said the old woman, "the hole will not close." And at once they closed it, and all of them came back together, the boys walking ahead of their grandmother. And such was the finding of the rubber ball.
